text:
The problem is that some people do not have access to their adult functions at will. Instead, they may go blank, access an inherited inner critic, or feel like a child part who may be playing at being an adult (what I call forced adulthood). Telling them to just access their adult is like telling a baby bird to just fly.

For that baby bird, I use a kind of provisional bridge (also found in Schema Therapy) that I call “borrowed adulthood,” which I'll detail here.

First, access your witnessing position if necessary, just noticing what’s there, without needing it to be warm or wise or certain. If you already know how to access different internal positions, move straight to the adult function you need to borrow.

If you have a safe adult in your life, you can borrow from them. If not, borrow from a mentor, an older brother/sister, your imagined future self, your god/goddess or higher power, a value you have, a plan you have written, etc. It’s ok to just borrow what you need right now, warmth or a boundary or direction, just like you would borrow a cup of sugar from a neighbor.

Next, put on your adult hat as if you are an apprentice adult, and pick the words or the action yourself. Then do at least part of it.

Last, return the adult hat, noticing what you borrowed and what you were able to do on your own (even if it’s only 5%).

The adult hat is only borrowed: the person you borrowed it from stays beside you, and you still make the choice. There is more on borrowed adulthood in my Inner Child Self-Love Reparenting Guide.

You don’t have to have trustworthy people in your history. Use someone you remember when that helps, or just imagine a good adult whose intention is to take good care of you. See if you can imagine what they would say/do in your situation, with your history, limitations, options, etc. If you can’t imagine a good adult, or just imagining a caring grown-up makes you feel more threatened, or lonelier, start smaller, with the least cruel response you can believe. Once you’ve found something good, try it out instead of repeating the exercise.

It can be helpful to use borrowing when you’re in the adult position and don’t know what a decent adult would do, especially when your inner child doesn’t trust you and every response you can think of is retaliating, defending your goodness, collapsing or leaving. How would a decent adult hear that distrust? Borrow that one response. You may still feel young when you do it. Feeling like an adult can come after you act like one.
section: No Adult Yet? Borrow One (under The Inner Adult's Three Jobs)
reader: Someone who has just read about the inner adult's three jobs and can't call up an adult in themselves at will: they go blank, hear their parent's critic, or feel like a child playing at being grown-up, and they need a way to act as the adult anyway, today.

checked.point: there is more on borrowed adulthood in the Inner Child Self-Love Reparenting Guide (and no longer a longer version of this exercise)
checked.found: The inner child guide as it stood on 2026-11-25 (catchup/INNER-CHILD-LIVE-20261125.md) has a section 'Borrowed Adulthood' under 'Building Your Inner Adult' ('I call it the “borrowed adulthood trick”'), with 'Borrow, Don't Sell Out' and 'One Skill at a Time' after it and, further on, 'Borrow Someone's Love', 'Borrow the Love You Give', 'Borrow a Guide to Build It' and 'Borrow Hindsight'. The words 'adult hat' are not in it, so the exercise told here is not there. He chose this wording (answer 8 a, 2026-11-25 11:18 UTC).
checked.still_needed: yes: they go there when the four steps here aren't enough, for the other things they can borrow (one skill at a time, love, a guide, hindsight) and for how to borrow without handing themselves over

placement: Where the author's own pointer stood: the second sentence of the paragraph that closes the four steps ('The adult hat is only borrowed ...'), before the two paragraphs on special cases (no trustworthy people in your history; borrowing when your inner child doesn't trust you). His sentence pointed back at 'this exercise', which had just ended; this one names the section's whole subject, and the section says more about it straight after. It still reads in order there, as the close of the steps, and nothing of his was moved. 'borrowed adulthood' points to the name he gives in the section's second paragraph ('that I call “borrowed adulthood,” which I'll detail here'); the sentence has no 'also', 'this' or 'as for'. The guide's title will be the link, to that guide's 'Borrowed Adulthood' section.

opens.first_sentence: The problem is that some people do not have access to their adult functions at will.
opens.why_reading: 'The problem is that some people do not have access to their adult functions at will.' names the reader's own case under the heading 'No Adult Yet?': they can't call the adult up on demand, and it is a known problem and not their failing. The next sentence gives the three states they would recognize (going blank, the inherited critic, a child playing at being an adult), so they know the section is for them.

same_point: none: read the section from its heading to the next for any other pointer to the inner child guide or to more on borrowed adulthood; this is the only one, and it takes the place of his sentence, so the section still has one pointer. Outside the section, 'It Feels Fake' in Troubleshooting gives a short form of borrowing; it points nowhere and is untouched.

marked.difference: 28, mild, and about its place more than its words: it says there is more on borrowed adulthood elsewhere, and then the section itself goes on with more on it for two paragraphs. His sentence in this place pointed at 'this exercise', which had just ended; a pointer for the whole subject would more naturally end the section.

kept.There is more on borrowed adulthood in m: The place is the author's own (his pointer stood here) and the wording is the one he chose (answer 8 a, 2026-11-25 11:18 UTC). It closes the steps, the part of the section the other guide tells differently, and the section's last line ('Feeling like an adult can come after you act like one.') is his ending, which a pointer after it would blunt. Moving it is his call; it is named in the subagent's report.

questions.Q1: PASS: 'There is more on borrowed adulthood' is the point, in the first six words; where it is comes after.
questions.Q2: N/A: the sentence gives no instruction; it says where more is and leaves going there to the reader.
questions.Q3: PASS: it names the one thing the other guide is offered for here, 'borrowed adulthood', in place of 'the longer version of this exercise', which that guide no longer has; and it names the guide by its title.
questions.Q4: PASS: 'borrowed adulthood' is the author's term, explained in the section's second paragraph where it is first used ('a kind of provisional bridge ... that I call “borrowed adulthood”'); 'my Inner Child Self-Love Reparenting Guide' is his other guide by name and will be a link to its 'Borrowed Adulthood' section.
questions.Q5: PASS: it follows the sentence that closes the exercise ('The adult hat is only borrowed ...'): the same subject, then where there is more on it.
questions.Q6: PASS: the steps come first and the pointer closes them, in the place the author's own pointer had. The read against his fixes marked, mildly, that the section says more about borrowing in the two paragraphs after it; kept there with the reason.
questions.Q7: PASS: this reader's case is having no adult to call on, and the other guide's sections on borrowing are for the same case; the pointer no longer promises an exercise that isn't there.
questions.Q8: N/A: the sentence sorts nothing into groups.
questions.Q9: PASS: one plain statement with its small words ('There is more on ... in my ...').

question_text.Q1: Why am I reading this sentence, and do I know it before I have to work through it? (the point first, in each sentence and each paragraph; a study after the question it answers; a term explained where it is first used, never in a sentence after it)
question_text.Q2: What is each instruction for, said in the reader's terms, and is it something the helper does ("have someone go with them"), not a rule stated as a fact ("someone goes with them")?
question_text.Q3: Which thing exactly? (pools of water, not water; any substance, not anything)
question_text.Q4: What does each word act on, or mean here? (adjunct remedy; known-genuine) Is every term a high-school graduate wouldn't know (enterocytes, BPC-157) explained once, where it is first used, and common ones (a vitamin) left alone? Is each mechanism explained by what it does in the reader's experience (dopamine "for motivation (by showing us what is important to pay attention to)"; DeltaFosB "preventing that learning from really clicking"), not by where it sits or what it looks like ("a chemical blanket", "the slower one underneath")? (E375)
question_text.Q5: Why does each sentence follow from the one before? (every but, so, because and this has what it turns on)
question_text.Q6: Is this the order the reader is thinking in, and does each idea sit next to what it continues?
question_text.Q7: Does each fact help this reader now, in their case (the same kind of thing they face, not just the same topic)?
question_text.Q8: Does each item belong in the group it is put in?
question_text.Q9: Is anything compressed? (one step a sentence, the small words that carry the relation, no space before mg)
